full_judgment:
Md. Imman Ali J: This reference forwarded by the learned Judge (District and Sessions Judge), Druta Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong, under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, seeks confirmation of the sentence of death imposed by him on Salauddin @ Tipu and Abdul Jabbar Lablu @ Labu (absconding) under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code. Accused Abdul Jabbar Lablu was tried in absentia. By the same judgment and order, five other accused persons, namely Abu Taher, Syed Nurul Azim Babar, Nurullah @ Marju, Biplob and Khalek were convicted under sections 302/34 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life and also to pay fine of Taka 50,000 each, and out of the money thus realised, 80% was directed to be paid to the father of the victim and the remaining 20% to be deposited with the government treasury. Condemned prisoner Salauddin @ Tipu preferred Jail Appeal No. 372 of 2004 as well as Criminal Appeal No. 903 of 2004. Convicted prisoners Abu Taher, Syed Nurul Azim Babar and Nurullah @ Marju jointly preferred Criminal Appeal No. 902 of 2004. Convicts Biplob and Khalek absconded throughout and are not appellants before us. The Reference and all the appeals arising out of the same judgment and order were heard together and are disposed of by this judgment.

2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that deceased Kamal Hossain (the victim) was an active worker of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and the accused persons threatened his life unless he joined the Awami League. On 31-8-2000 accused Abdul Khalek called the victim from his house saying that accused Abu Taher had called him to join the procession (মিছিল). After the procession the victim was dragged to the front of Abu Taher's house and, thereafter, to the front of the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union, where he was kicked by Abu Taher and assaulted variously by accused Abdul Jabbar Labu, Syed Nurul Azim Babar, Nurullah @ Marju, Biplob and Khalek. The victim was gagged and tied with ropes and the bones within his body were shattered using iron hammer, rods and pipe. At about 6-00 to 6-15 PM Md Alauddin, father of the victim (informant), heard that his son was in hospital. He, along with Abul Kashem (PW 2), went to the Emergency Unit of Laxmipur Hospital, where they found him in a dying condition. The victim made a dying declaration before his father and the witnesses naming the accused persons as his assailants. The victim was later taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where he died on 2-9-2000.

3. The informant lodged the first information report (FIR) on 25-10-2001 at 8-25 AM with Laxmipur Police Station, thus setting in motion Laxmipur PS Case No. 54 dated 25-10-2001. The informant explained in the FIR that he could not lodge the same earlier due to threats from the accused party who had surrounded his house and taken his signature on a blank piece of paper, threatening him that if he filed any case, he would be dead-meat for the dogs.

4. After due investigation police submitted charge sheet No. 121 dated 6-4-2002 naming 16 accused persons, alleging offences under sections 147/148/149/364/342/325/326/302/384/114/109 of the Penal Code. The case was registered as GR 959 of 2001 and was ultimately tried by the Druta Bichar Tribunal as Druta Bichar Tribunal Case No. 60 of 2003. During trial charge was framed against the accused, of whom seven were absconding, under sections 384/364/325/302/34 of the said Code, which was read over to the accused present in the dock, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. Trial in absentia was directed against the absconding accused.

5. In all 13 out of 14 prosecution witnesses produced were examined to substantiate the charges against the accused persons; no witness was called by the defence. From the trend of cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses and the statements made by the accused, when examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the defence case appears to be one of innocence and false implication. It is the positive defence case that the victim was killed by a mob having been caught as a snatcher/mugger and that the accused had been implicated through political motives.

6. Mr Md Yamin Newaz Khan and Mrs Shahnaz Haque, the learned Assistant Attorneys-General appearing on behalf of the State, placed before us the first information report, deposition of the witnesses and evidence and materials on record. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, Mr Mohammad Ali Akanda, appearing on behalf of the State, submits in favour of the Reference and prays for dismissal of the appeals and confirmation of the sentence of death. He submits that the prosecution witnesses vividly described the various stages from the time when the victim was taken from his house and, thereafter, made to take part in a procession and then taken forcibly to the house of accused Abu Taher, who is a renowned godfather of the area, and then, upon his order, he was mercilessly beaten, which culminated in his death. He submits that PW 1, the informant, described how his son, the victim, was taken from his house by accused Khalek, who had said that accused Abu Taher had ordered him to take part in the procession. He points to the evidence of PWs 3 and 4 who saw the victim being pulled away after the procession in front of the house of Abu Taher. Thereafter, PW 6 saw the victim being taken to the Rickshaw Sramik Union Office and PW 8 saw him being beaten up in front of that office. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that PWs 6 and 8 saw the actual assault upon the victim by the accused persons as detailed in their deposition. He then points out that after the victim was taken to the hospital he made a dying declaration in the presence of PWs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 11, all of whom narrated the contents of the dying declaration which implicated the accused persons in the assault of the victim. He also points out that PW 7 went to the hospital and saw the victim with his arms and legs broken. He submits that, although seemingly the contents of the dying declaration made to PWs 1 and 2 differ slightly, the difference is due to the fact that the victim answered separately to questions put to him, firstly by PW 1 and, thereafter, by PW 2. He submits that the Court is to look at the overall picture, as portrayed by the evidence of the witnesses, and to see whether or not the accused persons have been rightly convicted of the offence charged, based on the evidence produced. He submits that there is nothing wrong if the victim, in fact, gives more than. one dying declaration to different witnesses. He submits that the Court is to see whether the statement of the victim, as repeated by the witnesses as the dying declaration, can be believed. In support of his contenion, he refers to Surat Singh and another vs State of Punjab, AIR 1977 (SC) 705 where it was held that if there is more than one dying declaration there is no call to doubt the entire dying declaration. In that case the first dying declaration was accepted as true. He also refers to Jorubha Juzer Singh vs State of Gujarat, 1980 SCC (Cri) 316,

7. With regard to the delay in lodging the first information report, the learned Deputy Attorney General points out that the evidence of the witnesses clearly show that there was good reason why the first information report could not be lodged earlier, since the accused persons had threatened the victim with dire consequences if he proceeded with filing a case against them and also took signatures from the informant on blank paper, as seen from the evidence of PWS 1, 2 and 3. He submits that it is, therefore, natural that the informant would not take steps to lodge any information with the police while the accused persons are at large and wielding power.

8. Turning to the contention about the actual place of occurrence, the learned Deputy Attorney General points out that, although the witnesses have deposed that the occurrence took place in front of the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union or in front of the Bancha Nagar Tamijuddin Eidgah Math or in front of the banana stails, the place is one and the same and that there is no contradiction in the statement of the witnesses with regard to the place of occurrence. The difference in the narration arose only due to the angle from which the witnesses observed the occurrence. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also points out that when the, witnesses deposed to have visited the victim in hospital and narrated what the dying victim told them, there is no reason to disbelieve their evidence. He further points out that the fact that the victim was seriously injured is corroborated by the doctor (PW 9), who produced in Court evidence of the treatment given by him to the victim at the Emergency Unit of Laxmipur Hospital.

9. Finally, the learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the prosecution has been able to prove the case against the accused persons with cogent and credible evidence and there is no reason to interfere with the judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial Judge.

10. Mr Md Munsurul Hoque Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of appellants Abu Taher, Salauddin @ Tipu and Nurullah @ Marju in Criminal Appeal No. 902 of 2004, submits , that the whole prosecution case is a concoction and filed only to gain political benefit. He points out that the falsity of the prosecution case becomes apparent immediately if one looks at the inquest report dated 2-9-2000. He points out that the occurrence allegedly took place on 31-8-2000 and the victim died in Dhaka on 2-9-2000 and the inquest was held by the police of Ramna Police Station, DMP., Dhaka on the same day. It is apparent from the inquest report that at the time of the inquest the informant was present and witnessed the inquest. It is also apparent from the report that Alauddin, father of the victim, told the official conducting the inquest that on 31-8-2000 at about 6-00 PM., while his son (the victim) was standing by the side of the Bancha Nagar Tamijuddin Eidgah Math, 7/8 persons with the intention of killing him, assaulted him on various parts of his body with rod, thus causing serious injury upon his legs, arms and other parts of his body. The learned Advocate points out that the first information report., which was lodged after almost 14 months, discloses a different place of occurrence and also names persons not named at the time of inquest, who are alleged to have assaulted the victim. He points out that the inquest was held immediately after the death of the victim and by that time the informant, being the father of the victim, had already been made aware by his son, by way of his dying declaration, about the names of the persons who had inflicted the injuries upon his body and, therefore, there was no excuse for not naming the accused persons when asked by the police at the time of the inquest. In this regard, reference was made to Shahin Ahmed vs State, 12 BLC 165, where it was observed that disclosure of the names of the convict-appellant by way of dying declaration stood flung to the wind by inquest report as the persons to whom the dying declaration was alleged to have been made were present at the time of the inquest and were signatories to the inquest report, but did not disclose the name of anyone as the victim's assailant, The learned Advocate further points out that the place of occurrence has been shifted to either in front of the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union or inside that office, with a view to giving the occurrence a political colour. He submits that had any such occurrence taken place at the place now alleged, there was no reason to mention a different place as the place of occurrence when the inquest was held. The learned Advocate submits that the explanation of the witness that the delay in lodging the first information report was caused by threats held out by the accused persons is not tenable in view of the fact that at the time of the death of the victim and when the inquest was held, the informant was in Dhaka, far away from Laxmipur where he was alleged to have been under threats. The learned Advocate points out that it is apparent from the evidence of PW 1, that he had sufficient courage to go to the police in order to register a GD on 2-9- 2000, being Ramna Police Station GD Entry No. 107. He submits that the prosecution subsequently, suppressed that particular GD Entry, wherein no accused persons were named, as that would have nullified the prosecution case against the accused persons. He points to the order sheet of the trial- Court, wherein it is seen that the defence filed an application for the production of the GD Entry Register containing GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000. However, the Register was not forthcoming, and ultimately, the police produced and filed a spurious photocopy alleging the same to be a copy of the GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000. The learned Advocate points out that the prosecution had done its utmost to suppress the original GD by resorting to producing a photocopy, when the original GD Register was admittedly in existence. The Special Public Prosecutor certified that he saw the original GD with his own eyes, but refrained from producing it in Court without assigning any reason. The learned Advocate submits that if the original GD Register existed and if the Special Public Prosecutor had seen the same sitting in Chittagong, then there was no reason why the original Register could not be produced before the Court.

11. Mr Munsurul Hoque points out that although PW 9 deposed before the Court and stated that he treated the victim at the Emergency Unit of Laxmipur Hospital, the evidence on record would show that he could not have done so had he been a real genuine practitioner. The learned Advocate points out that the papers produced by PW 9 marked as Exhibit X (with objection) were admitted into evidence illegally since they are photocopies of records of the hospital and could not be produced as secondary evidence without any explanation as to why the primary evidence, namely, the original record of the hospital, could not be produced. Furthermore, it appears from the evidence of the doctor that he carried out an operation on the victim without taking any X-ray, although he himself had directed X-ray is to be done. The learned Advocate points out also that the first information report mentions that the informant took his son to two hospitals and also mentions that the doctor gave his son preliminary treatment, but no mention was made of any operation having been carried out. He also points out that there was no evidence produced with regard to the transfer of the victim from the hospital in Laxmipur to the Dhaka Medical College Hospital. The learned Advocate points out that the photocopied papers produced cannot be taken to be eividence of the admission, treatment and discharge of the victim from that hospital. It being a government hospital, there ought to have been original records produced in Court in support of the prosecution case. He submits that the prosecution evidence with regard to the hospitalisation of the victim in Laxmipur is not at all substantiated. The learned Advocate submits that in the absence of any evidence of hospitalisation, the prosecution story that the victim made any dying declaration at a hospital cannot be believed. Moreover, he points out that the dying declaration is not at all a dying declaration in the eye of law, inasmuch as the statements made by the witnesses do not reflect the actual statement made by the victim. Each of the witnesses has described the narration by the victim in a different way, naming different assailants and different weapons used to cause the injuries. The learned Advocate points out that the dying declaration is not in the language of the victim and, according to the evidence of PW 1, there is no mention of the presence of accused Taber. The learned Advocate further points out that, according to the evidence of PWs 1 and 2, they both went to the hospital at the same time, but when giving evidence they stated two different versions of dying declaration of the victim. He submits that the evidence of the witnesses with regard to the dying declaration is not credible. He also points out that PWs 3, 4 and 6 did not mention the name of Salauddin @ Tipu, although they are witnesses of the dying declaration. He submits that the variation in the narration and names of the assailants as stated by the different witnesses, calls into serious doubt the credibility of the dying declaration.

12. The learned Advocate points out that the time of the occurrence is also not substantiated by the evidence of the witnesses, inasmuch as PW 1 stated to have received information about his son's hospitalisation at 6-00 to 6-15 PM, whereas in the first information report he stated that the victim was left at the hospital at 6-50 PM, which raises a doubt as to how he could have received a message at 6-15 about his son's hospitalisation. The learned Advocate points out that in the first' information report names of certain witnesses are stated but no reason is given for their inclusion in the first information report as witnesses and there was no indication of their presence at the time of occurrence. Since the position or location of the witnesses at the time of occurrence, vis-a-vis the place of occurrence, is not mentioned in the first information report, it leaves it open for them to depose during the trial according to the need of the prosecution. He also points out that PW 3 deposed in Court to have witnessed part of the occurrence and also the dying declaration, but his name was not mentioned in the first information report nor Was he examined by the police under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure until about four months after the first information report was lodged although in his deposition he stated that he had been present in Laxmipur from 31-8-2000 to 30-11-2001. The learned Advocate submits that the failure to lodge any first information report contemporaneously and the reasons given by the informant for the delay are not credible since the police outpost is seen to be only 15 yards away from the house of accused Taber, where the victim was first dragged away from the procession. If it is admitted that there was a procession on the date of occurrence and a serious beating took place, this would naturally result in the police finding out about the occurrence and going to that place. The learned Advocate submits that the prosecution has suppressed that part of the story. Moreover, there is no reason why the informant could not have lodged the first information report with Ramna Police Station when he was/ in Dhaka away from the threats of the accused persons. Furthermore, he points out that after the then government in power ceased, there was a period when the neutral Caretaker Government took over, but the informant took no steps even at that time to lodge the first information report.

13. The learned Advocate points out that the prosecution case of a hammer being used to cause the injuries on the body of the victim resulting in his bones being shattered is not borne out by the evidence of the doctor, who conducted the post mortem examination. He did not find any broken bones and only found lacerated wounds and bruises, which thus belies the prosecution story as deposed by the witnesses. He submits that the occurrence took place in broad daylight in a public place and it was a market day. There were independent witnesses, shopkeepers and employees who could have been called by the prosecution to depose. But the prosecution chose only to produce witnesses who originated from the village of the victim. He further points out that the occurrence took place allegedly in front of the banana stalls and one banana stall owner was a charge-sheeted witness and examined by the police, but he was not produced before the Court and no explanation was given for the failure of the prosecution to produce him as a witness. He submits, therefore, that the prosecution has failed to substantiate the case against the accused persons and they are entitled to be acquitted of the charges leveled against them. He prays that the appeals be allowed.

14. Mr Md Abul Bashar, the learned Advocate appearing as State Defence Lawyer on behalf of absconding convict Abdul Jabbar Lablu alias Labu, adopts the submissions made on behalf of condemned prisoner Salauddin @ Tipu. In addition, he points out that the place of occurrence, according to the first information report, was the Rickshaw Sramik Union Office, whereas in the charge the place of occurrence has been noted as the torture chamber adjacent to accused Taher's house and, therefore, the charge is defective. He also submits that there is a misjoinder of charge, inasmuch as there ought to have been individual charge against each individual accused person. The learned Advocate points out that the prosecution's explanation regarding the delay in lodging the first information report cannot be accepted where the delay has been for one year and two months and the police station is only 200 yards away from the place of occurrence. He submits that when such an occurrence took place there must have been information to the police and the police must have come to the place of occurrence having recorded a diary, but the prosecution withheld the real story. The learned Advocate further points out that the surathal report does not name any accused persons, although by that time the names of the assailants had been known by the informant, as he had heard about the occurrence from the victim himself and had been told the names of the accused persons. The learned Advocate submits that the prosecution must prove the case with regard to place, time and manner of occurrence and there must be a clear finding of the Court in this regard, as was held in the case of Abdul Karim vs States another, 1981 BLD (AD) 200. He also refers to Alkas Mia and others vs State; 25 DLR 398 and submits that non-examination of independent witnesses, when they would naturally have been available, should lead to an adverse inference being drawn against the prosecution under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. He submits that the place of occurrence being a market place there would have been permanent shop owners who would have been disinterested and competent witnesses, but they were not examined. He refers to Habibullah and others vs State, 21 DLR (SC) 88 and submits that, where the first information report is belated, it is unworthy of credit and that statements of witnesses made shortly after the occurrence would carry more weight.

15. Mr Abdul Malek, the learned Advocate appearing along with Mr SM Shahjahan, learned Advocate on behalf of appellant Syed Nurul Azim Babar, adopts the submissions made on behalf of the other appellants. He further submits that there was no overt act of this appellant as disclosed in the dying declaration of the victim, only PW 8 disclosed the complicity of this appellant but only in a general manner. The learned Advocate, referring to State vs Paron Chandra Baroi and Paran Chandra Baroi vs State, 2 BCR 292, submits that the inquest report is admissible in evidence, and in this case speaks volumes about the non-complicity of the accused persons in the occurrence alleged. He points out that the informant, who was a witness to the inquest, was specifically questioned by the police at that time, but failed to name the accused persons. He submits that this negates the whole prosecution case. He submits that the inquest report shows the place of occurrence to be a place other than the one now sought to be proved by the prosecution and the inquest report, being the earliest narration in point of time, has a greater value than the deposition of witnesses, who have been primed in the meantime to support the prosecution case. The learned Advocate points out that the inquest took place in Dhaka and thus there was no possibility of any threat hanging over the head of the informant when' he answered the questions of the police at the time of the inquest. He submits that if the contents of the inquest report are believed then the prosecution case totally falls apart. He submits that the appellant is liable to be acquitted of the charges levelled against him and prays that the appeal be allowed.

16. Let us now consider the evidence and materials on record, as produced by the prosecution in order to prove the charges levelled against the accused persons.

17. The informant Md Alauddin, father of the victim, deposed as PW 1, narrating the prosecution story more or less as stated above. He stated that his son was called out of the house on the order of accused Abu Taher to join the procession and subsequently at 6-15 PM he received news that his son was in hospital. He, along with Abul Kashem (PW 2), went to the Emergency Unit at Laxmipur Hospital where they found the victim in a dying condition. In answer to his query, his son told him that Labu and Tipu caused his injuries by beating him with a hammer. The witness stated that his son's arms and legs were broken. Accused Biplob, Babar and Marju tied the hands and legs of his son and accused Khalek bunged his mouth with a cloth. He stated that his son was subsequently taken from Laxmipur Hospital to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where he died on 2-9-2000. He proved the first information report (Exhibit 1), which he lodged on 25-10-2001, wherein his signature is marked as Exhibit 111. In his cross-examination; he stated that he lodged a typed first information report. He denied the suggestion that there was any theft case against his son or that there was land dispute between his son and the accused persons or that there was any scandal relating to any affair with any women. He asserted that at the time of the occurrence accused Taher was the Pourashava Chairman and a god father in the area. He admitted that Nurul Islam had been abducted after the occurrence involving his son. He stated that he could not go to the police after the occurrence because the accused persons kept him under observation and also he did not go to the Court. He admitted that at one point there was a Caretaker Government and also the Army used to patrol the streets. He denied the suggestion that a person in a dying condition cannot speak. He stated that there was no hartal in Laxmipur on 31-8-2000 and that he did not know why his son went to join the procession. He admitted that between 31-8-2000 and 25-10-2001 he consulted Advocates about the matter. He admitted that he did not see the occurrence himself and that at the time when his son made a dying declaration to him, a doctor was present. He admitted that none from the market place was a witness in this case. He admitted also that witness Abul Kashem is from his homestead. He stated that his son had been admitted to the hospital in Laxmipur and his name is in the register, but he could not remember whether he gave the investigating officer any papers relating to the hospitalisation. He denied the suggestion that his son had not at all been admitted in Laxmipur Hospital. He admitted that he has a shop in the market place. He denied the suggestion that he had included the name of accused Taher and his family members having been influenced by others. He admitted that he did not go to the Army Camp in order to report the occurrence. He denied the suggestion that his son died for reasons other than those described by him in the first information report and that he signed the first information report at the behest of the Officer- in-charge. He stated that his house is 5/7 minutes away from the place of occurrence and that the police station is 5 minutes away. He stated that at the time when his son was beaten up he screamed. On recall, the witness stated that on the order of accused Abu Taher, his son was taken to the north side of the banana stalls into the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union where his arms and legs were broken. He also stated that he took preparations to lodge the case, but then accused Taher and the other accused surrounded his house and threatened to kill him if he lodged any case against them and that they would throw his flesh to the dogs. He also stated that accused Taher and his cohorts obtained his signature on blank paper. In his further cross-examination he admitted that at the time of the inquest he was present and at that time he did not see any person belonging to the Taher group. He admitted that he may have said that 7/8 persons beat his son with iron rod by the side of the Eidgah Math, but then said that he could not remember having said so. He stated that he did not name Taher as accused in fear that he could not go back to Laxmipur. He stated that in his GD Entry No. 107 he did not name any accused. He also stated that his younger brother Harun had a shop in the market place. He denied having mentioned before the Court about the presence of a doctor at the time when his son was giving the dying declaration.

18. PW 2, Haji Abul Kashem, stated in his deposition that on 31-8-2000 he went to the market place and saw a procession. At about 7 in the evening he was told by Alauddin that his son is dying at the hospital. He went with Alauddin to the hospital and found the victim crying in front of the Emergency Unit. When he asked about his condition, the victim told him that he was taken to the Rickshaw Sramik Union Office where accused Taher kicked him and, thereafter, Tipu, Marju, Babar tied him and accused Labu struck him with a hammer on his legs. When he screamed, accused Khalek bunged his mouth with cloth and accused Tipu beat him with pipe while accused Lablu was beating him with a hammer. Accused Taher intermittently kicked him. Accused Goni, Shipon, Kalek, Tipu, Labu and Taher together assaulted the victim and made him disabled. Accused Marju took him and left him at the hospital. The witness also stated that after the burial, when the informant took steps to file the case, accused Taher, Shuman, Biplob, Shipon, Khalek and Goni surrounded the house of Alauddin and forbade him from filing any case on the threat of killing him and burning down his house. The accused also took the signature of the informant on a blank piece of paper. In his cross-examination, he stated that he often met the police between 31-8-2000 and 25-10-2001 and twice met the Investigating Officer (10). He stated that he told the Investigating Officer what he heard from the victim. He stated that the hospital was half kilometres away from the place of occurrence. He stated that at the time when he was speaking to victim Kamal, there was no doctor present. He denied the suggestion that he did not at all go to the hospital on that day nor spoke to Kamal. He stated that he told the Investigating Officer that Taher intermittently kicked the victim. He stated that it was market day on Thursday and that the shops remained open until 8.00 PM. He also stated that after being treated in Laxmipur Hospital, the victim was admitted into a private clinic. He denied the suggestion that the police had escorted him from Laxmipur to the Court (in Chittagong) so that he would depose falsely in support of the prosecution case. He denied the suggestion that the accused did not beat the victim as deposed by him.

19. PW 3, Abu Siddique and PW 4, Md Selim deposed as eyewitnesses of the occurrence. PW 3 stated that he saw a crowd of people in front of the house of Taher Mia and observed that Biplob, Labu, Babar and others were pulling victim Kamal, trying to take him to the house of Taher. When they reached that place, Taher Mia came out of his house and told them to take him inside and to fix him and he at the same time told the other people present, to go away. The witness stated that he heard in the evening that Kamal was in hospital. He went to the hospital where, upon questioning by his father, Kamal stated that Biplob and Labu demanded arms from him and that Taher kicked him to the ground and Labu struck him with a hammer on his legs and arms, Biplob, Labu, Tipu and others beat him after gagging his mouth. In his cross-examination he stated that he went to the Emergency Unit of the Sadar Hospital where he saw Kamal and after hearing his statement he went back. He denied the suggestion that he did not tell the investigating officer about the beating of the victim with hammer, He denied the suggestion that he was deposing falsely and that Kamal died as a result of beating by the public. PW 4 deposed in a similar fashion and stated that when he went to the place in front of Taher's house, he saw Biplob, Lablu, Babar, Marju, Goni, Shipon and Rinku pulling at victim Kamal, whereupon Taher Mia came out of his house and told them to take him inside the house and to 'size' him. He heard in the evening that Kamal was in hospital where he went and saw Kamal's father and other people present and when his father asked him, Kamal replied that Biplob, Labu, Babar, Marju, Goni, Rinku and others beat him with hammer. In his cross-examination, he stated that the police outpost is about 100 to 150 cubits from the Banana Stalls. He stated that he did not know where the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union was located. He also stated that the police station is 150/200 cubits from the house of Taher Mia. He denied the suggestion that he did not narrate to the 10 about the presence of Kamal's father and Haji Saheb at the hospital or about the victim naming the accused, He stated that Kamal did not narrate the occurrence at different times and that he narrated the same at one and the same time. He denied the suggestion that he did not tell the Investigating Officer about accused Biplob, Marju and Goni beating the accused with hammer.

20. PW 5, Ohid Mia, was tendered by the prosecution and in his cross-examination by the defence he denied that he was the President of the BNP of the local Ward. He stated that he did not see the occurrence.

21. PW 6, Humayun Kabir and PW 8, Abdur Rahim narrated the occurrence in a similar fashion stating that they saw the occurrence which took place on 31-8-2001 at 5-30/6-00 PM. PW 6 stated that when he reached Tamijuddin Eidgah Math he saw 8/10 persons, including Taber Mia, Biplob, Babar, Labu, Khalek, Goni and Rinku, taking the victim from the house of Taher Mia towards the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union. While he was being taken inside the office, Taher Mia said to 'size' him up and out of the accused persons, a number of them beat the victim with hammer and iron rod. He thereafter left the place. In his cross- examination, he stated that he was examined by the police one year and eight months after the occurrence and that between 31-8-2000 and 15-1-2002 he was present in Laxmipur and during that period he met with police, but in that period he did not disclose the occurrence to the police. He stated that the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union is about 4/5 cubits wide and has a door 4 feet tall and that when the door is closed the inside is not visible. In his further cross-examination, he denied the suggestion that Kamal was caught while mugging and died as a result of public beating. PW 8, stated the time and place of occurrence as 5-30 PM in front of the Sramik Union office" where he saw Babar, Biplob, Tipu, Labu and 7/8 other persons assaulting Kamal upon the order of Taher Mia to beat him. In his cross-examination, this witness also stated that he was present in Laxmipur between 31-8-2000 and 15-1-2002 and that the police recorded his statement in the year 2002. He denied the suggestion that he did not tell the Investigating Officer about seeing Taher Mia standing outside the Rickshaw Sramik Union Office. He also denied the suggestion that Kamal was caught mugging and died as a result of public beating.

22. PW 7, Nazimuddin, went to the hospital at 7-00 PM where he saw Kamal with his legs and arms broken. He also stated that after Kamal's death, the accused obtained the signature of Kamal's father on blank paper. In his cross-examination he denied the suggestion that he himself was a cohort of Kamal in his gang of thieves.

23. PW 9, Dr Md Nuruddin, deposed that on 31-8-2000 he operated upon the victim Kamal having admitted him in the Orthopaedic Ward of the hospital. In his cross-examination, he stated that he could not remember the name of the doctor who admitted him and that he had advised for the victim to be X-rayed, but as there was no X-ray machine in the hospital he carried out the operation without any X-ray report. He admitted that he did not give any discharge certificate for this patient and it is normal for the doctor who carried out the operation on a patient to give the discharge certificate. He denied the suggestion that he did not carry out any operation on Kamal or that he had been forced to give false evidence.

24. PW 10, Abu Bakkar Siddique, is the first Investigating Officer who received the typed first information report from the informant Alauddin along with admission certificate, injury certificate and copy of chalan, copy of inquest and copy of the post mortem report relating to the victim Kamal. He filled up the first information report form and registered the case. He proved the first information report (Exhibit 1), wherein his signature is marked as Exhibit I (2) and his signature in the first information report column is marked as Exhibit 1(3). Upon receiving instruction to investigate the case, he went to the place of occurrence, prepared the sketch map (Exhibit 5) and index (Exhibit-6), wherein his signatures are marked as Exhibit 5(1) and 6(1) respectively. He examined the witnesses and recorded their statements under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On being transferred, he handed over the case docket to his successor. In his cross-examination, he admitted that when an injured person is admitted in a government hospital he is given an injury certificate and that states the case history of the injuries. He stated that the first information report was lodged 13 months 24 days after the occurrence and in the meantime there was a Caretaker Government. He also admitted that when the police station does not accept any case then the case may be lodged directly with the Magistrate. He stated that according to the inquest report, it was prepared upon description received from the victim's father and that in it, it is stated that 7/8 persons beat him with iron rod in order to kill him and that the said inquest report contains the signature of the victim's father. He stated that he gave evidence in the Nurul Islam murder case and that case was started during the period of BNP rule. He admitted that he did not examine any shopkeepers or any persons from the Rickshaw Sramik Union nor any person from the hospital. He admitted that in the place of occurrence market place there is a Press Club and Police Outpost, but he was not aware who was in charge of the Police Outpost at that time. He denied that since he did not investigate the case in accordance with the demand of the government, he was removed from the case.

25. PW 11, Md Siddique, is a witness to the oral dying declaration, who stated in his deposition that when he went to the hospital he saw Kamal's father (PW 1), Haji Abul Kashem (PW 2), Siddique (PW 3), Selim (PW 4) and many others. Kamal told them that Labu, Biplob, Babar, Marju and 10/15 others beat him with iron rod and hammer and broke his arms and legs and sent him to the hospital. In his cross-examination, he stated that he met up with the police 1-1(1/2) years after the occurrence and that the police asked him to go to the police station, but he was not aware how the police came to know that he was aware of the occurrence. He admitted that he had never been to the police station to inform about the occurrence. He admitted that he did not disclose about seeing Haji Abul Kashem, Siddique and Selim at the hospital. He also admitted that he told the police having heard about the occurrence, but did not inform the investigation officer as to from whom he heard it. He denied the suggestion that he was a hired witness and that he was deposing falsely at the behest of the Public Prosecutor and the Member of Parliament of Laxmipur. He denied the suggestion that Kamal died as a result of receiving public beating after being caught mugging.

26. PW 12, SI Mosharraf Hossain, is a Police Officer who was posted at the Ramna Police Station at the relevant time, held the inquest on the body of the victim, which was identified to him by the victim's father Alauddin. He proved the inquest report (Exhibit 2), wherein his signature is marked as Exhibit 2(1) and the chalan (Exhibit 3), wherein his signature is marked as Exhibit 3(1). In his cross- examination, he admitted that the inquest report shows in paragraph 3 that 7/8 persons assaulted the victim and that the place of occurrence is written as by the side of the Eidgah Math where the victim was standing and that he was beaten with iron rod. He admitted that the victim's father was present at the time of the inquest. He stated that GD Entry No. 107 was written by the Officer on Duty and that the same is still at Ramna Police Station.

27. PW 13, Dr Mostaque Rahim, deposed in support of the post mortem examination report (Exhibit 4), wherein his signature is marked as Exhibit 4( 1). He found the following injuries.

i.	One lacerated stitched wound on the front of left mid-leg measuring 1-1/2" x 1/2" x muscle depth.

ii. One lacerated stitched wound on the left upper leg 1/2" x 1/2" x muscle.

iii. One lacerated stitched wound on the right lower leg 2" x 1/2" x bone.

iv. 	Lacerated stitched wound on the right lower leg 1-1/2" x 1/2" x bone.

v. One bruise from right elbow to right wrist joint 13" x 2" with dislocation of right elbow joint.

vi. Another bruise from left shoulder to left hand 22" x 3" with dislocation of left wrist.

28. In his opinion, death was due to haemorrhage and shock as a result of the above mentioned injuries which were ante mortem and homicidal in nature.

29. In his cross-examination, he admitted that it is necessary to carry out X-ray to confirm diagnosis and that if plaster was applied on a broken bone without taking X-ray that would be medical malpractice. He also stated that laceration means (থৈতলা জখম).

30. PW 14, Kamrul Hasan, is the second Investigating Officer, who stated in his deposition that he examined witnesses and recorded their statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and perused the case docket and upon finding prima facie case, submitted the charge sheet against 16 named accused persons. In his cross-examination, he stated that he did not know in how many cases the victim was an accused. He admitted that it appears that in Laxmipur Police Station Case No. 13 dated 7-5-1996 under sections 379/411 the victim was an accused. He stated that he did not ascertain whether any GD had been lodged at his police station with regard to the murder of Kamal. He did not examine the Medical Officer who was on duty at the Sadar Hospital at the time of occurrence. He admitted that he did not examine any office bearer of the Rickshaw Sramik Union or any Member of the Traders Association or of the Members of the Press Club. He did examine Masum and Bellal, an owner of the banana stall. He admitted that the witnesses were examined almost 11/2 years after the occurrence. He stated that the first information report mentions assault by hammer and fist blows, but does not make any reference to any other weapon, nor about any specific dates when the house of the informant was surrounded or threats made upon him. He stated that he found during investigation that Kamal was dependent on his father. From his further cross-examination it appears that the witnesses did not mention to him about the presence of accused Taher at the place of occurrence. He denied the suggestion that the victim died under different circumstances and that he was influenced by the Minister, Public Prosecutor and local Member of Parliament to include the accused persons in the concocted charge sheet.

31. In the light of the above evidence, the learned trial Judge found the accused persons guilty and convicted and sentenced them as aforesaid.

32. We have perused the evidence and materials on record and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates. The occurrence took place, as alleged, one year and two months before the first information report was lodged at the local police station of Laxmipur. The explanation given for the delay, that the informant was unable to lodge any information with the police due to the threats by the accused party, seems somewhat tenuous in view of the fact that there was a Caretaker Government for a period prior to the lodging of the first information report when there could not have been any political pressure upon the informant not to lodge the first information report. Furthermore, we find its lange the police station and outpost being so close to the place of occurrence that the police personnel manning those stations did not care to investigate such a serious occurrence, which took place almost at their doorstep, in broad daylight. On the other hand, if they had taken notice of such an event, the prosecution has suppressed that side of the story. Moreover, it appears that another murder took place in the same locality, namely Nurul Islam murder, which was reported to the police and investigation and trial held soon thereafter. We also note that the informant, according to his own admission, recorded GD Entry No. 107 at Ramna Police Station on the date when his son died in Dhaka, but he did not go so far as to file any regular first information report there narrating the occurrence. We are inclined to accept the submissions of the learned Advocates for the appellants that at that time there would not have been any pressure on the informant from any quarter to prevent him from lodging the first information report at Ramna Police Station. We find from the evidence that no member of the accused party was present when the inquest took place at Dhaka Medical College Hospital. On the contrary, we find that the informant, upon being questioned by the Police Officer holding the inquest, told his that the occurrence took place by the side of the Eidgah Math when 7/8 persons beat his son with iron rod. No mention of any names of the accused persons was made at that time. We note that the informant, in his cross-examination, did not deny his statement to the Police Officer at the time of inquest and initially admitted the same and, on second thought, prevaricated by saying that he could not remember what he said at that time. However, he was a signatory as a witness to the inquest report. We also bear in mind that section 179 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for lodging information with any police station within whose jurisdiction the occurrence took place or any consequence ensured. In the instant case, the consequence of the occurrence culminated in the death of the victim in Dhaka and, therefore, the informant was at liberty to lodge information with the police in Dhaka. If there was any situation preventing him from lodging any information with the local police station, he could have lodged the information elsewhere. Thus, we do not find satisfactory explanation of the delay of about 14 months in lodging the first information report. Moreover, in the event of the police refusing to take his ejahar, there was always the possibility of the informant filing a complaint petition before a Magistrate, who would treat the same as ejahar.

33. We find the evidence of PW 1 that he admittedly registered GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000 with Ramna Police Station, wherein he did not name any accused persons in spite of the fact that the occurrence had allegedly been narrated to him in detail by the victim, naming the assailants. It transpires that several attempts by the trial Court to see the Register containing that GD Entry ended in failure and resulted only in an attested photocopy being submitted in Court and accepted by the trial Judge. We shall deal with the GD Entry at a later stage. Suffice to say at this stage that admittedly the informant did not name the accused persons in his GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000.

34. With regard to the alleged oral dying declaration made by the victim at Laxmipur Hospital, we find there is material variance between the statement allegedly made by him to PW 1, the informant and that made to PW 2, who admittedly went to the hospital at the same time as the informant. The statement made to PW 1 was also alleged to have been heard by PWs 3 and 4, but still there is material difference between the statement heard by PW 1 and that heard by PWs 3 and 4. If all three witnesses heard the same statement made before them at the same place and at the same time then they would depose in Court giving the same narration as given by the victim. We also cannot accept the explanation that two separate statements would have been made to two witnesses giving differing details, bearing in mind that both the witnesses are stated to have gone to the hospital at the same time. We bear in mind the deposition of PW 4 that the victim only made one statement while they were there. We also note that PW 1 stated that at the time when the victim made his dying declaration there was a doctor present, but he retracted from his statements in further cross-examination, whereas PW 2 stated that when the victim made his statements there was no doctor present. Such backpeddling by PW 1 within a space of the one month appears to be motivated and geared to corroborate PW 2 who deposed differently in the interim period. If there was a doctor present then it would have been the prosecution's duty to produce that doctor as an independent witness to support the dying declaration, and that has been avoided by PW 1 later by back-tracking about his earlier statement in Court regarding the presence of the doctor at the time of the dying declaration. PW 3 narrated how, in answer to question posed by his father (PW 1), the victim gave the dying declaration stating that Biplob and Labu demanded arms from him, where as PW 1 did not mention any such statement by the victim. The discrepancies and contradictions highlighted in the various dying declarations as narrated by the witnesses, leads us to believe that no such dying declaration was made at the time as alleged.

35. With regard to the injuries alleged to have been caused upon the victim, we find from the evidence of the witnesses that a heavy hammer was used to break the arms and legs of the victim. We note that the witnesses described how the bones of the victim had been shattered. However, from the post mortem examination report, we do not find any broken bone in the whole of the body of the victim. Only lacerated wounds are detailed by the post mortem examination report as well as bruising, which do not, therefore, corroborate the prosecution story with regard to the manner of occurrence, inasmuch as we do not find that any injuries caused by use of a heavy hammer was found on the body of the victim. With regard to the evidence of PW 9 the doctor, who allegedly operated upon the victim., we are of the view that his evidence is somewhat suspect, particularly in view of the fact that only photocopies of papers were produced in support of his statement that he operated upon the victim. Where the original record is still likely to be kept at the hospital; it being a government hospital, there is no provision for producing photocopies of such documents. We are of the view that the learned Judge was clearly wrong in admitting such evidence into the record. Such admission of evidence is clearly contrary to provisions of the Evidence Act. Moreover, we note that PW 9, who allegedly operated on the victim, did not mention any broken bones found during the operation on the victim.

36. With regard to the evidence of the alleged eyewitnesses, we find that the descriptions given by them with regard to the narration of the assault by the accused upon the victim with various weapons, is very much discrepant. We do not find any consistency in the descriptions given. The place of occurrence has not been fixed to any particular place, inasmuch as some of the witnesses alleged that the occurrence took place in front of the office of the Rickshaw Sramik Union and some said that the occurrence took place inside the office, whereas we find from the earliest recorded evidence, namely the inquest report, that the occurrence took place by the side of the Tamizuddin Eidgah Math. We are inclined. to put more weight on the description as narrated in the inquest report, since it is more contemporaneous and is the earliest available information regarding the occurrence. In this particular case, we note that the informant PW 1 was confronted with his earlier statement, as made by him at the time of inquest, and that he initially admitted the same, but then, on second thought, prevaricated by saying that he could not remember what he said earlier. Nevertheless, the inquest report is a valuable piece of evidence and, it having been signed by the informant as a witness and admitted into evidence during trial, we rely upon this evidence. In this regard we take support from the Paran Chandra Baroi case, cited above. The decision of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division in Bangladesh (State) vs Paran Chandra Baroi,6 BCR (AD) 225. In the more recent case of Shahin Ahmed, cited above, it was observed, upon citing several decisions of our Supreme Court and the Indian Supreme Court, that statement in the inquest report is admissible in evidence.

37. The witnesses who deposed in this case, apart from one, all originate from the village of the victim. In a case of this nature, where the occurrence took place in broad daylight in a market place, it would be essential for independent and competent witnesses to be brought in support of the prosecution case. It appears that one owner of the banana stall, which is in front of the alleged place of occurrence, was examined by the police, but he was withheld as a witness in this case. it is admitted that many other persons who would have been present at or near the place of occurrence, it being a market day, have not been cited as witnesses nor examined during the trial and, particularly when the police examined the witnesses admittedly 14 and 18 months after occurrence, we are inclined not to place much reliance upon the evidence of such witnesses.

38. The whole of the prosecution case hinges on the allegation that the victim was a supporter of BNP and that he was being forced to join the Awami League and, due to his failure to join the Awami League, he was done to death by the supporters of the Awami League at the time when the Awami League Government was in power. However, from the evidence on record, it appears that the victim neither held any post in nor was an office-bearer of any political party in the locality. The only slight evidence that we have shows that he merely supported a political party. It has not been shown what benefit such a single non descript supporter of a political party would bring to the opponent party. We cannot find that the motive of killing him for refusal to join any other particular party is at all made out in the facts and circumstances of the case.

39. With regard to the GD Entry, which was admittedly made by the informant at Ramna Police Station, being GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000, we find that several attempts were made by the Court to get a sight of the original GD Entry Register, but the same was not produced before the Court. The prosecution took the alternative course of producing a photocopy of the same, which was attested by the then Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station. We also note that the learned Special Public Prosecutor engaged in the case addressed a letter to the Court dated 26-2-2004 stating that he had seen with his own eyes the original GD document made at Ramna Police Station relating to death of victim Kamal, of which an attested copy had been produced and the genuineness was under challenge by the accused. As the Special PP who represented the State, he was certifying that there was no reason to believe that it was unattested or imaginary. He prayed that the document placed on behalf of the State be accepted as genuine and admitted by the Court. We have ourselves scrutinised the photocopy of the GD which is found within 'File B' of the lower Court's records at page 364. The photocopy appears to have been attested by the Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station DMP, Dhaka on 3-3-2004. The concerned GD Entry No. 107 is couched in between the GD Entry Nos. 106 and 108 and 109 appearing on the same page. The date 2/9/2000 appears at the top of the page. At first glance there seems to be nothing untoward. However, on close scrutiny, it appears that the photocopy certainly could not be a photocopy of a page from a General Diary Register. We note with grave concern that the GD appears to be written on a page of a general diary printed form supplied by Bangladesh Government (BG) Press, having printed material written on top and bottom of the page with margins drawn on both sides and bearing page numbers, place for entry of date, etc. However, the hand-written GD Entry appears to be upside down in relation to the printed BG Press form. We are clear in our mind that the piece of paper produced as an attested photocopy of the GD Entry is spurious and has been falsely fabricated for the purpose of this case in order to ensure the conviction of the accused persons.

40. We ourselves took steps, with the help of the learned Deputy Attorney-General, to have the original GD Register containing GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000 brought from Ramna Police Station, DMP, Dhaka to this Court for our perusal. The incumbent Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station initially responded by saying that the GD Register could not be traced and that perhaps, it had been destroyed. On the date next fixed for hearing of the appeal, he appeared before us with an Inspection Register Book of Ramna Police Station, wherein it is recorded that the GD Entry Registers up to and including the year 2000, along with Command Certificate (CC), were destroyed on 14-12-2006. We have perused the Inspection Register produced by the Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station, AKM Doulat Akbar. We note that the pages of the Register are in shambles, having no proper sequential page numbering and having many blank pages containing some handwritten notes and some typed pages pasted in the Register. We also find many pages half filled with notes and other half remaining blank. We also find pages torn out of the Register without any endorsement as to their tom condition. Certainly the state of the Register does not engender any confidence with regard to its contents and veracity. In response to our direction, the officers concerned in destroying the earlier records submitted an affidavit of facts giving details of the destruction of the Registers, etc. It is stated in the affidavit of facts sworn by Md Taherul Huq Chouhan, Assistant Superintendent of Police, who destroyed the General Diary Registers, that he undertook such destruction on the order of the Deputy Commissioner of Police. In support, he filed a Circular (Annexure-A), which had been sent to all the police stations on the instruction and direction of the then Commissioner of Police, DMP, Dhaka. The document produced as Annexure-A, which is placed before us as justification for destruction of the GD Registers of Ramna Police Station, relates to an inspection of New Market Police Station by the then Police Commissioner. He found that police station in total disarray and disorder. He observed so many irregularities in the functioning of that office and preservation of their records and documents, that he ordered the officer-in-charge of that police station to put his station in order within 7 days, including the destruction of old GD Registers more than 5 years old and Command Certificates more than 2 years old. Having given his directions to the officer-in- charge of that station concerned, he directed the Deputy Commissioner, Head Quarter and Deputy Commissioner, Supplies to report to him having followed all the instructions mentioned by him earlier, within 7 days. Then the. Commissioner listed a number of other actions to be taken by other police stations and he directed all the DC(s) and AC(s) of all Police Stations within DMP to submit weekly out-turn of work and those reports to include details of matters mentioned within serial 1 to 14 of his memo. We do not find, within those matters listed in serial No.1 to 14, anything relating to destruction of GD Registers or Command Certificates preserved by other police stations. Therefore, the explanation that the GD Registers at Ramna Police Station were destroyed on the basis of the circular now produced before us is untenable. If the GD Entry Registers at Ramna Police Station had, in fact, been destroyed, then, apart from the provisions of the PRB to retain records for up to 5 years, we do not find any legitimate order for the destruction of the said GD Registers. Incidentally, it may be pointed out that the note purportedly recording the destruction of the Registers, mentions some Rules from the PRB which have no connection with destruction. We may also mention in passing that in Death Reference No. 109 of 2004, heard and disposed of by this Bench on 31-7-2007, we had occasion to peruse the original GD Registers of Lalbagh Police Station, DMP, Dhaka for the year 1998. Obviously the aforementioned circular did not lead to destruction of the Registers in that police station.

41. Therefore, in view of the above, the Inspector General of Police is directed to make inquiries into the matter of the legality and propriety of destruction of GD Registers kept at Ramna Police Station.

42. We are also of the firm view that the attested photocopy of the page of the GD Register, purportedly containing GD Entry No. 107 dated 2- 9-2000, produced before the Court, was an exercise in fabrication of false evidence for the purpose of the case and, therefore, we propose to take action against the then Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station, who attested this spurious documents as a genuine copy, as well as the Special Public Prosecutor, who declared to have seen the corresponding original document and vouched for its authenticity.

43. In view of the above discussions, we are satisfied that the prosecution has not been able to prove the case against the accused persons with evidence from competent and reliable witnesses and genuine documentary evidence, beyond reasonable doubt and the accused persons are liable to be acquitted of the charge leveled against them.

44. In the result, the Reference is rejected. Criminal Appeals No. 902 of 2004 and 903 of 2004 are allowed. The judgment and order of conviction and sentence is hereby set aside. Jail Appeal No. 372 of 2004 is accordingly, disposed of.

45. Appellants Abu Taher, Syed Nurul Azim Babar and Nurullah alias Marju in Criminal Appeal No. 902 of 2004 and condemned prisoner-appellant Salauddin alias Tipu in Criminal Appeal No. 903 of 2004 are acquitted of the charges leveled against them and may be released forthwith, if not wanted in connection with any other case.

46. Since accused Biplob and Khalek have been absconding throughout the trial and are fugitives from justice and are not appellants before us, we refrain from passing any observation as to their guilt in the commission of the offence.

<u>47. It appears prima facie that Md Mahabubur Rahman, the then Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station, on 3/3/2004, fabricated false evidence by way of making a photocopy of a GD Entry, which he attested as true copy of the GD Entry Register. Such an act by the officer-in-charge can be brought within the mischief of sections 193/194/195 of the Penal Code, since the evidence was used in the trial to secure conviction of innocent accused for commission of an offence involving the death penalty. It further appears that Ahmad Kamrul Islam Chowdhury, who at the relevant time was engaged in the trial of the instant case as Special Public Prosecutor, Chittagong, took positive steps to testify to the genuineness of the attested photocopy of the GD Entry declaring that he had seen the original GD document. The falsity of their respective attestation/declaration is evident from a cursory glance at the photocopy which shows the original printed form to be upside down.</u>

48. In view of the above, Mr Abdur Razzaque Dewan, Deputy Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh is directed to file a petition of complaint before a competent Magistrate in pursuance of the provisions laid down in section 195(1)(b) read with section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against Md Mahabubur Rahman, now Inspector, Officer-in-Charge, Thanchi Police Station, Bandarban, for commission of an offence of fabricating evidence, namely, making a photocopy of a page of a GD Entry Register, purportedly of GD Entry No. 107 dated 2-9-2000 of Ramna PS, DMP, Dhaka, attesting the same as a true copy, intending thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause the conviction of the accused, thereby constituting an offence punishable under sections 193/194/195 of the Penal Code and against Mr Ahmad Kamrul Islam Chowdhury, Advocate of the Chittagong Bar for, vouching for the authenticity and veracity of a palpably forged attested copy of a GD Entry, stating that he had seen the original document, thus constituting an offence under section 196 of the Penal Code.

<u>49. It may not be out of place to mention that a question may be raised at the time of taking cognisance by the Magistrate as to whether sanction is required under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecuting a public servant who is not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government. Firstly, an Offices-in-Charge of a police station does not fall in this category as Government sanction is not required for his removal from service. Secondly, in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the provisions of section 197 would not be attracted in any event since the act alleged to have been done constituting an offence was certainly not done while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, In no way does the act of fabricating evidence have any nexus with the Official duty of the officer concerned as contemplated in section 197 of the said Code. The learned Magistrate is to take a note of this aspect of law accordingly.</u>

50. Let a copy of this judgment be transmitted to the Inspector General of Police for information and for taking necessary action in view of our observations and directions above in respect of the destruction of records at Ramna Police Station on 14-12-2006.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.
